title: 3-Read Friday #56: Direct Instruction Strands, AI and Artisan Teaching, and Motivation
author: Craig Barton
summary: The first issue of 2025 opens with a New Year's greeting and three picks spanning curriculum design, AI, and motivation research. Barton recommends Dylan Kane's account of teaching multiple 'strands' of content per lesson, an idea borrowed from Direct Instruction's 'tracks', connecting it to his own memory of reading a Connecting Math Concepts teacher's guide. He then highlights Becky Allen's essay on generative AI and the future of 'artisan teaching', tying it to what he calls his 'current obsession' with AI saving teachers time. His third pick is Natalie Wexler's summary of research showing achievement predicts motivation more reliably than the reverse, which he frames as a direct answer to teachers' constant question of how to motivate students.
points: Barton's own surprise at Direct Instruction's 'disconnected strands' structure -- contrasted with the single-theme lesson he expected -- shows him actively updating his mental model of what good curriculum sequencing looks like, not just passively linking to Kane's post.
He explicitly names AI-for-teacher-time-saving as an ongoing personal 'obsession', linking back to his own Tips for Teachers newsletter content on 'messing about with AI'.

His summary of the Wexler pick states the counterintuitive finding precisely: achievement predicts motivation, but motivation doesn't reliably predict achievement -- reversing the folk assumption that motivation must come first.

Bundling a curriculum-sequencing piece, an AI-and-teacher-workload piece, and a motivation-research piece in one issue reflects Barton's habitual mix of classroom-craft, technology, and cognitive-science recommendations.
quotes: Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
Dylan shares his experiences of trying to implement this approach in his teaching.
Regular readers will know that using AI to save teachers time and help them do their jobs better is a current obsession of mine.
How to motivate students is a question teachers constantly ask ourselves.
This post by Natsalie provides a great overview of motivation research.
One finding comes through loud and clear: Achievement consistently predicts motivation, but motivation does not predict achievement.
